If f_n converged uniformly to g, then it would converge pointwise to g, hence g=f by uniqueness. With epsilon 1/2, uniform convergence would require strict inequality |f_n(x)-f(x)|<1/2 for all n>=N and x in [0,1]. Choosing x=2^{-1/N} gives x in [0,1), f(x)=0, and |f_N(x)-f(x)|=x^N=1/2, contradicting that requirement. The listed group-theoretic rules are irrelevant and are not used.","unresolved_conditions":[],"counterexample":null}

{"problem": {"theorem": "Define $f_{n}:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by the equation $f_{n}(x)=x^{n}$. Show that the sequence $\left(f_{n}\right)$ does not converge uniformly.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "topology", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "target": {"node_id": "n1", "version": 2}, "target_node": {"text": "\begin{proof}
For each $x\in[0,1)$, we have $x^n\to0$, while $f_n(1)=1$ for every $n$. Thus $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to the function
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Suppose that $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to some function $g$. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, so uniqueness of pointwise limits gives $g=f$. Taking $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$, uniform convergence would yield an integer $N\ge1$ such that $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\tfrac12$ for every $n\ge N$ and every $x\in[0,1]$. Set $x=2^{-1/N}<1$. Then $f(x)=0$ and
\[
|f_N(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\tfrac12,
\]
a contradiction. Hence $(f_n)$ does not converge uniformly on $[0,1]$.
\end{proof}", "claim": "The sequence $f_n(x)=x^n$ has pointwise limit $f=0$ on $[0,1)$ and $f(1)=1$, and a fixed epsilon witness contradicts uniform convergence to this necessarily unique pointwise limit.", "scope": [], "depends_on": [], "goal_refs": ["main"]}, "closed_predecessors": [], "counterexample_search": true, "rule_candidates": [{"id": "grp_normal_quotient", "name": "Quotient group criterion", "statement": "If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.", "conditions": ["N is a subgroup of G", "N is normal in G"], "conclusion": "G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.", "rule_digest": "f6d458aa2e7463efeea7a535cdbe0f0f7930259cfe7f845b5350ec03454da876", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "grp_first_iso", "name": "First isomorphism theorem for groups", "statement": "If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "conditions": ["phi is a group homomorphism", "ker(phi) is the kernel of phi"], "conclusion": "G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "rule_digest": "335c687d26f64e41584f1b8bc575aec9d78223b01c4821bf0056bf8533de0c19", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "grp_lagrange", "name": "Lagrange theorem", "statement": "If G is a finite group and H is a subgroup of G, then |H| divides |G|.", "conditions": ["G is finite", "H is a subgroup of G"], "conclusion": "|H| divides |G|.", "rule_digest": "361a6b53eb7c1cb71cc90836aab9022d76163052528c559907341ebabe9bf547", "applicability": "unchecked"}]}
